title: Fulfill your contracts
hook: O you who believe, fulfill your obligations (5:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isa in the Qur'an's telling: a messenger, a word conveyed to Maryam, a spirit from Him. Your line was a word from him. Did you read the verses slowly? Day three hundred eighty-eight, and a new surah.

The fifth surah is al-Ma'idah, the Table Spread. It takes its name from a story near its end, where the disciples of Isa ask for a table of food to come down from heaven. Tradition places it among the last surahs revealed. And it opens with a command of two Arabic words, three in Pickthall's English, right after the address. No story, no setting. Just a sentence that covers a marriage, a mortgage, a handshake, and a treaty.
screen: `AL-MA'IDAH, THE TABLE SPREAD.` → `AMONG THE LAST REVEALED.` → `ONE SHORT COMMAND.`

segments.voice: Here it is, 5:1, in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Fulfil your undertakings." The Arabic for undertakings is al-'uqud, contracts, plural of 'aqd. Arabic dictionaries trace it to a root for tying a knot. A contract is a knot tied between two parties, and the verse says: don't let it slip. Commentators read 'uqud widely: the covenant between a person and God, and every agreement between people, marriage, sale, rent, employment, oaths, treaties. Marriage itself is called 'aqd al-nikah, the knot of marriage. Elsewhere, in 17:34, the Qur'an adds that the covenant will be asked about. The Prophet ﷺ faced a hard test of it at Hudaybiyyah. He had just agreed a treaty with the Quraysh of Mecca, and one of its terms was painful: anyone who came over from Mecca to the Muslims without permission would be sent back. The ink was barely dry when a young Muslim named Abu Jandal stumbled into the camp in chains, escaped from Mecca, begging not to be returned. His own father, Suhayl, was the Meccan who had negotiated the treaty. The companions were in anguish. He kept the terms, and told Abu Jandal to be patient, that God would make a way out for him. The sira reports that the way did open: before long, the Quraysh themselves asked for that clause to be dropped. A contract kept only when it's convenient isn't really a knot. The verse asks for one that holds even when it pinches.
screen: `'AQD: A KNOT TIED BETWEEN TWO` · `WITH GOD, AND WITH PEOPLE` · `ABU JANDAL IN CHAINS` · `A KNOT THAT HOLDS WHEN IT PINCHES` · then, large: `FULFIL YOUR UNDERTAKINGS.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, list in your mind the knots you've tied. A lease. A job. A promise to a friend. A deadline you agreed to. A commitment to a spouse or a child. A small one, like I'll call you back. Notice which knots are holding and which have quietly slipped. Don't punish yourself. Just pick one agreement you'll keep to the letter this week, especially one that's become inconvenient. Picture keeping it. The bell holds the time.
Fulfill your contracts. Awfu bil-'uqud: keep the knots you've tied, with God and with people, the opening of al-Ma'idah, 5:1. Today's word.
Your line: keep the contract. Today, keep one agreement to the letter, on time and in full, even the small ones, like I'll call you back. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims treat contracts as religious obligations: marriage is concluded by an 'aqd, Islamic commercial law rests on honoring agreements, and 5:1 is often quoted on keeping promises and treaties.

what a scholar hears: 'aqd from '-q-d, to tie; the basis of Islamic contract law; and Hudaybiyyah as a hard test of it.
